How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability).

Provenance, kept so that a TRACE Research Object (TRO) declaration of the run can be written later from a stored result (metacheck #404; the helpers are in R/provenance.R). Only when code was run (execute = TRUE): * run_results$started_at, run_results$ended_at: when each run of a script started and ended (ISO 8601, UTC, milliseconds); NA for a script that was not started. A script run again in a later pass has the times of its last run. A TRO uses them for each trov:TransparentResearchPerformance. * run_results$exit_status: the exit status of the process that ran the script (0 = ended normally); NA when the process did not report one (a time limit, or Docker failing to start the container). * artifacts: one row per file, with stage (deposit: as downloaded from the repository, hashed from the downloaded file; before_run: the run folder just before the first script ran, after metacheck’s own changes, such as rewritten paths and unpacked archives; after_run: only the files the scripts made (status new), changed (changed) or removed (removed), as an unchanged file is the one listed before the run), path (relative to the run folder, as valid UTF-8, a byte of another encoding written as <xx>), size (bytes), sha256, mime_type (by extension, NA when unknown), source (the file’s address in the repository, for deposit). The package libraries metacheck installs in the run folder are left out, as are metacheck’s own files there (a script’s runner, and the statistical output it writes in statistical_output/). Files metacheck itself copied or made between passes (see modifications, output_copied, file_placed) show in after_run too. A TRO uses the rows as trov:ResearchArtifacts and each stage as a trov:ArtifactArrangement. * modifications$sha256_before, modifications$sha256_after: the hash of the changed script as downloaded and as it ran; NA when the script is not at the same path in both (a script made from an R Markdown file). * environment: the system that ran the code (trov:TransparentResearchSystem in a TRO): metacheck_version, started_at, ended_at, host (R version, platform, operating system), sandbox, network_isolated (TRUE only when every Docker run had --network none; the process sandbox does not stop the network), internet, timeout_per_script, total_timeout, python_local (the Python run outside Docker and its version), and docker: runs (for each kind of run, r_run, r_install, python_run, python_install, the image and the docker run arguments, such as --network none, --read-only, --cap-drop ALL, no-new-privileges, the process limit and the memory and processor limits) and images (for each image, its ID and digests from docker image inspect, its creation time and the R and Python versions its environment declares).

run_results$checked says what the run of each script shows about the code, in five groups, so that a script that does not reproduce is kept apart from one the check could not test: ran (it ran to the end); code_error (it did not reproduce: it stopped with an error of the code or the deposit, could not be read, or needs a file the deposit does not hold); dependency (a package or program was not available: a package that could not be installed or was not loaded, a program outside R and Python, a system library, or R crashing in a package’s compiled code); time (it did not finish within the time limit for one script, or was not started because the time for all scripts had run out); and not_checkable (it could not be checked automatically: it needs a person, the internet, a key or another setting of the authors’ computer, one platform such as Google Colab, Windows or OpenSAFELY, more memory than the run allows, a file that was not downloaded, a screen, or a program that runs it, or it is a file of a package of the code that Python runs only as a module of that package). It is NA for files run inside another script, files that are not an analysis, files not read, and a Docker failure. summary_table counts each group (repro_ran_n, repro_code_error_n, repro_dependency_n, repro_time_n, repro_not_checkable_n), and the report’s first sentence gives them. The traffic light reflects the static readiness signals by default; a script in code_error that stopped with an error makes it red, as a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure, and a script in one of the other three groups keeps it from being green. Calls that need a screen, which the run does not have (dev.print(), dev.copy2pdf(), dev.copy2eps(), savePlot(), windows(), win.graph(), x11(), quartz(), View()), are replaced before the run by calls that need none, which modifications records as screen_call_replaced. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

The authors would like to thank Will Lucas for his support with survey creation and administration.

Ethics approval and consent to participate: Study procedures were approved by the Behavioral Health Research Collective Institutional Review Board (#047) and carried out in accordance with the provisions of the World Medical Association Declaration of Helsinki.

Written verbal consent was obtained for all participants.

Introduction

Self-transcendent experiences are a broad class of altered states of consciousness that lack a single, widely accepted definition. They have been variably described as feeling "connected to something larger than or outside of your everyday sense of self" (Garcia-Romeu et al., 2015), as "transient mental states of decreased self-salience and increased feelings of connectedness" (Yaden et al., 2017a), and as an inherently human orientation toward values, meaning, or causes beyond the self (Frankl, 1966). Self-transcendent experiences are closely related to philosophical and contemplative concepts, such as Thich Nhat Hanh's notion of "interbeing"-the profound interconnectedness and interdependence of all things (Hanh, 2017), as well as spiritual, mystical, religious and sacred experiences (MacLean et al., 2012; Stace, 1960). Self-transcendent experiences may also entail deeply felt positive mood (Pahnke, 1963) and self-transcendent emotions (e.g., awe, compassion, gratitude) (Cova & Seragnoli, 2025)-a category of positive emotion that involves attention beyond one's self, such as to the needs of others, thought to have a salient social bonding and altruism function (Gordon et al., 2017).

Self-transcendent experiences are often experienced as profoundly meaningful and transformative (Griffiths et al., 2008) and can elicit a range of downstream intra-and interpersonal benefits (Gordon et al., 2017; Griffiths et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2023). They are believed to contribute to wellness and meaning in life (e.g., Frankl, 1966) and are thought to be central to the efficacy of several interventions for wellbeing and mental health, including mindfulness and contemplative practices (Hanley et al., 2020; Verhaeghen, 2019; Wong, 2016). In psychedelic-assisted therapies, in particular, self-transcendent and "mystical-type" experiences have been repeatedly implicated as candidate mechanisms of therapeutic change (van Elk & Yaden, 2022; Yaden & Griffiths, 2021). Psychedelic compounds reliably occasion intense forms of self-transcendent and mystical experiences, regarded as central explanatory constructs in their therapeutic effects (Romeo et al., 2025).

Psychedelic-assisted therapy research frequently treats mystical and self-transcendent experiences as a holistic phenomenon. For instance, the Mystical Experience Questionnaire (MEQ30; MacLean et al., 2012)-one of the most commonly used measures of mystical-type experiences within the psychedelic literature (De Deus Pontual et al., 2023)-is most often indexed by its global score (Romeo et al., 2025), which averages across mystical experience, positive mood, transcendence of time/space, ineffability subscales. While this total score and measures of 'complete mystical experience' have often shown robust associations with psychedelic-assisted therapy outcomes (Barrett et al., 2015; McCulloch et al., 2022; Romeo et al., 2025), the MEQ30's validated subscales, based on earlier phenomenological analysis of mystical reports across cultures and traditions (Stace, 1960), 1 are often overlooked. In addition to the MEQ30 global score combining multiple facets of experience, so too do its subscales. For instance, the mystical experience subscale taps into experiences of insight, a sense of eternity, spiritual elevation, feelings of unity, heightened awareness, and transcendence from self-limitations. Similarly, the 5 Dimension Altered State of Consciousness scale (5D-ASC, Studerus et al., 2010)-another commonly used measure of subjective experience in the psychedelic field-combines multiple facets of self-transcendent experience. For instance, the experiences of unity subscale spans a sense of global oneness, oneness with one's surroundings, and with past/present/future, alongside a sense of touching eternity, and feeling that conflicts and contradictions dissolving. The higher-order oceanic 1 Stace's (1960) argued that unity is central to mystical experience and distinguished two fundamental forms: extrovertive unity (perceiving an underlying unity within the external world) and introvertive unity (an ineffable experience of undifferentiated oneness involving dissolution of ego, subject-object distinctions, and sensory content). The MEQ30 was designed to reflect these and related features, including nontemporal and nonspatial qualities, inner subjectivity (a sensed inner presence or reality in all things), a noetic quality, a sense of sacredness, ineffability, and paradoxicality.

boundlessness dimension, a mystical construct similar to the MEQ30 total score (Liechti et al., 2017), spans positively experienced depersonalization, experience of unity and deeply positive mood. Even narrower measures blend multiple dimensions of experience; for instance, the Ego Dissolution Inventory assesses distortions in the subjective sense of self alongside a sense of interconnectedness/oneness (Nour et al., 2016).

While such blended measures of mystical-type experiences provide an important bigpicture overview of broad dimensions of experience, theory and empirical work suggest that self-transcendent experiences and feelings of unity are not unitary but encompass overlapping though dissociable facets (Garcia-Romeu et al., 2015; Yaden et al., 2017a). For instance, empirical research has found that that only certain states, those characterized by a 'mystical' quality, sense of connection, expansion or positive mood, are associated with beneficial outcomes, whereas experiences predominated by time and space distortions, ineffability, and small self-size or ego dissolution appear less so or not at all (Barrett et al., 2015; Kałużna et al., 2022; McCulloch et al., 2022; Tyson et al., 2022; Yaden, 2020a). Based on a review of constructs with a self-transcendent experience component, Yaden and colleagues (2017) proposed a broad theoretical distinction between experiences characterized by an annihilational or 'self-loss' component-marked by loss or attenuation of a bounded sense of self-and those characterized by a relational or 'connection' quality-involving felt connection with others, humanity, or the world. Overall, while the emphasis on global, mystical-type experiences (e.g., MEQ30 total, 5D-ASC oceanic boundlessness) in psychedelic research may capture the often-blended nature of psychedelic experiences, it may also obscure meaningful phenomenological dimensions that are relevant for clinical change and for optimizing therapeutic context.

Although recent work has begun to elaborate theoretical frameworks for organizing types of self-transcendent and mystical experiences (Cova & Abatista, 2025; Stocker et al., 2024), a cohesive and widely accepted delineation and operationalization of self-transcendent experience types-and their differential relevance for therapeutic outcomes-remains lacking. The current study sought to address this gap by clarifying higher-order dimensions of psychedelic-occasioned self-transcendent experiences and examining whether these distinctions have practical and psychological significance, with the goal of supporting more precise and conceptually parsimonious measurement. To this end, we conducted an exploratory factor analysis to identify higher-order components of psychedelic-occasioned self-transcendent experiences across several measures relating to self-transcendent experiences and examined how these components relate to mindset at the time of substance ingestion, negative acute experiences, and persisting positive psychological effects.

Methods

The pre-registered secondary data analysis (https://osf.io/a4f9e) is part of a broader online observational study comparing mystical and self-transcendent experiences while under the influence of cannabis, MDMA and psilocybin. Full study details and sample characteristics have previously been described (redacted-for-anonymous-review). Briefly, 397 adult participants reported on an experience with cannabis (n = 131), MDMA (n = 133), or psilocybin (n = 133) in the past 5 years that was at least of a moderate subjective intensity.

In the present study, all analyses were run with the full sample given that substance type had a small impact on self-transcendent and related experiences (redacted-for-anonymizedreview). Participants had a mean age of 34.3 years (SD = 9.5). Gender was 60% men, 38% women, and 2% nonbinary. The sample was 59% white, 29% Black or African American, 10% Hispanic or Latinx, 8% Asian, 1% Indigenous/American Indian, and 2% mixed race.

Data and associated code for the present study are available online (https://osf.io/ayjgh). Study procedures were approved by the [redacted-for-anonymized-review] Institutional Review Board (redacted-for-anonymized-review) and carried out in accordance with the provisions of the World Medical Association Declaration of Helsinki.

Measures

Primary Purpose for Use

Because the majority of the sample (83%) endorsed recreational purposes (redactedfor-anonymized-review), we created a binary variable coded as 1 for therapeutic or healing purposes (treating a mental or physical health condition, self-improvement, spiritual reasons, or deepening a connection) and 0 for non-healing or recreational purposes. Supplementary Appendix A presents additional measures information.

Intentions and Mindset

Measures assessing intention and mindset at the time of substance ingestion that were identified as predictors of psychedelic-induced mystical experience in a systematic review were administered (Aday et al., 2021). Five items assessed spiritual-prosocial motivations (Russ et al., 2019). Internal reliability was excellent in the current study (α = .94). Two items assessed clarity of intentions (Haijen et al., 2018). A single-item adapted from (Russ et al., 2019) assessed apprehension prior to substance use. Four items from (Russ et al., 2019) assessed a state of surrender. Internal reliability was good in the current study (α = .81).

Negative Emotions

Negative emotions (upset, hostile, ashamed, nervous, afraid) during the substance use experience were assessed with the negative emotion subscale adapted from the International Positive and Negative Affect Schedule -Short Form (Thompson, 2007), a widely used measure of affective states that has shown good reliability and validity in diverse populations (Merz et al., 2013; Navarrete et al., 2025). Internal consistency in the current sample was good (α = .85).

Persisting Positive Effects

Persisting positive changes attributed to the substance use experience were assessed using four items adapted from the Persisting Effects Questionnaire-a commonly used approach to assess enduring positive and negative effects attributed to psychedelicoccasioned experiences (Griffiths et al., 2011 (Griffiths et al., , 2016 (Griffiths et al., , 2019;; McCulloch et al., 2022).

Participants were asked whether the experience or their contemplation of that experience has led to long-term and persisting changes in their: 'personal well-being or life satisfaction', 'life's purpose', 'mood' and 'behavioral changes.' Items were averaged into a composite persisting positive effects score to reduce pairwise comparisons; internal consistency was excellent (α = .91).

Measures Used in Factor Analysis

Self-Transcendent Experiences. The 9-item Self-Transcendent Experiences Survey (Yaden, 2020a) was included in the current study because it specifically assesses selftranscendent states without blending other related constructs (e.g., spiritual or religious experiences, noetic qualities). Five items assess self-loss self-transcendent experiences (sample item: "I felt my sense of self completely fade away"; α = .90 in the current study) and five assess connection self-transcendent experiences (sample item: "I had the sense of feeling closely connected to everything"; α = .94 in the current study) (Yaden, 2020a). This scale has shown good convergent, discriminate and predictive validity in initial validation work (Yaden, 2020a).

Self-Transcendent Emotions.

Five items adapted from the modified Differential Emotion Scale (Fredrickson et al., 2003b) were selected to assess the peak intensity of a range of self-transcendent emotions (awe, gratitude, inspiration, love, and sympathy) during the substance use experience. Items were intercorrelated (ρs: 0.52-.70, ps < .001) and averaged in the current study because a confirmatory factor analysis run using lavaan (Rosseel, 2012) supported a one-factor model of positive self-transcendent emotions (standardized factor loadings on the single latent factor: 0.77-0.89). Internal reliability was excellent in the current study (α = .90).

Mystical Experiences.

The Mystical Experiences Questionnaire (MEQ) was designed to assess various facets of mystical experiences that may result from hallucinogen use (MacLean et al., 2012). We administered the widely-used 30-item version (MEQ30), which has demonstrated good reliability and construct validity in past work (Barrett et al., 2015; Wirsching et al., 2024). The MEQ30 has four subscales: transcendence of time and space (sample item: "Loss of your usual sense of time"), ineffability (sample item: "Sense that the experience cannot be described adequately in words"), positive mood (sample item "Experience of ecstasy"), and mystical experiences (sample item: "Gain of insightful knowledge experienced at an intuitive level"). These subscales and the total score demonstrated good internal reliability in the current study (αs = .84-.97). Per convention (Griffiths et al., 2018), scores were calculated as a percentage of the maximum possible score, and thus could range from 0-100.

Small Self.

Participants responded to four items adapted from (Piff et al., 2015). The three assessing vastness relative to the self (sample item: "I felt the presence of something greater than myself"; α = .94 in the current study) were averaged separately from the single item assessing self-diminishment (sample item: "I felt small or insignificant"), because in prior work these facets of small self have loaded onto distinct factors (Tyson et al., 2022; Yaden et al., 2018) and shown distinct associations with outcomes, such as self-esteem, selfperspective, and ethical decision-making (Tyson et al., 2022).

Self-Other Overlap. The Inclusion of Other in the Self Scale (IOS; Aron et al., 1992) is a widely used single-item pictorial measure of interpersonal closeness, administered in the current study to assess self-other overlap. This measure presents a series of Venn diagrams depicting increasing overlap between self/others; participants in the current study were asked to select the picture that best described "how connected you felt with other people during the experience." Responses range from 1 (no overlap) to 7 (mostly overlapping), with a N/A (I was not with others) option available. In its original validation study, the IOS demonstrated alternate-form and test-retest reliability, convergent validity and discriminant validity, and predictive validity for later relationship outcomes (Aron et al., 1992). Subsequent research has supported its construct validity, showing strong correlations with other measures of relationship closeness (Gächter et al., 2015).

Statistical Analysis

Consistent with our prior methodology (redacted-for-anonymized-review), a small amount of missing data (1-4 responses on seven variables used in the present analyses) was imputed using predictive mean matching via the mice package in R (Van Buuren & Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011).

We next examined descriptive statistics, inspected correlations (Spearman given some observed skew) amongst measures, and examined the suitability of our data for factor analysis; the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) test of sampling adequacy (KMO = .90) and Bartlett's test of sphericity (χ²(45) = 2950.41, p < .001) indicated that the data were wellsuited for factor analysis.

We conducted an exploratory factor analysis (EFA) using the ten scales or subscales (if a measure had subscales) described above: self-loss and connection self-transcendent experiences, self-transcendent emotions, MEQ30 subscales (transcendence of time and space, ineffability, positive mood, mystical experiences), small self (vastness and selfdiminishment), and self-other overlap. Because measures were administered on distinct scales, variables were z-score standardized.

Best practices for EFA were followed when deciding upon extraction method, rotation method, and factor retention criteria (Goretzko et al., 2021). To determine the number of factors to retain, we examined the scree plot, conducted a parallel analysis, and examined factor loadings and overall variance explained by factor solutions. A maximum likelihood EFA was run, with promax and oblim rotations compared on the basis of explained variance, theoretical parsimony of factor solution, and model fit indices (Tucker Lewis Index (TLI), RMSEA (Root Mean Square Error of Approximation) index, Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC)). Indicators were then removed one-by-one from the factor analysis until a stable solution was identified. First, indicators with very low communality scores (< .20) were removed (Costello & Osborne, 2005; Samuels, 2017). Next, indicators were removed that most strongly violated the .40-.30-.20 rule (i.e., did not load onto primary factor above .40, the alternative factors below 0.30, or demonstrated a difference >0.20 between primary and alternative factor loadings) (Howard, 2016).

Once the final factor solution was determined, individual regression-based factor scores were calculated (McNeish & Wolf, 2020). Zero-order correlations between factors and other study variables were examined; given that some variables showed skew, Spearman correlations were used. We then ran a series of regression analyses with the regression-based factor scores together predicting various dependent measures: negative emotions (Model 1), positive persisting effects (Model 2), state of surrender (Model 3), apprehensiveness at time of substance ingestion (Model 4), clarity of intentions (Model 5), spiritual-prosocial motivations (Model 6), and primary purpose for use (Model 7). Across models, multicollinearity was not observed (VIF values < 2). For Model 4, an ordinal regression was used. For Model 7, a binomial logistic regression was used. For the remainder of the models, which had continuous dependent measures, linear regression assumptions were tested. Across models, some heteroscedasticity was observed; as such, robust standard errors were used. For models in which the assumption of normality of residuals was violated (per examination of diagnostic plots), generalized linear models (negative binomial, gamma, Tweedie) were tested for improved model fit. For Model 1, a negative binomial model best fit the data. For Models 2, 3, and 5, linear regressions best fit the data. For linear regression models, adjusted R² values are presented; for other models, McFadden pseudo R² was calculated with the pscl package (Jackman et al., 2015).

Results

Factor Analysis Findings

Supplementary Appendix B presents correlations between study variables. The scree plot and parallel analysis suggested that a 1-2 factor solution may best fit the data. Both were tested and compared, with a two-factor solution with oblimin rotation selected due to significant model fit improvements and greater theoretical parsimony. Supplementary Appendix C presents the scree plot, parallel analysis, and details on the selection of a twofactor solution.

The small self-self-diminishment item was removed first from the EFA because it showed low communality (h² = .14), indicating little variance explained by the factor solution. Next, the mystical experiences subscale was removed from the EFA due to high loading on the alternative factor (0.64 on the primary factor, and 0.40 on secondary). Finally, the vastness relative to the self-subscale was removed due to low discrepancy in factor loadings between the primary and secondary factor (0.51 and 0.34, respectively).

The final two-factor solution explained 67% of the total variance (37% for Factor 1 and 30% for Factor 2) and demonstrated good fit (RMSEA index = 0.09, TLI = 0.96, BIC = -11.63). Table 1 presents the finalized standardized loadings. The first factor was comprised of the connection self-transcendence, mystical experiences, self-transcendent emotions, and inclusion of self in other subscales and accounted for 35% of the total variance. This factor was consequently named "Connection and Positive Emotions." The second factor was comprised of the self-loss self-transcendence, transcendence of time and space, and ineffability subscales, and accounted for 32% total variance. This factor was consequently named "Time, Space and Self-Transcendence." The extracted factors were moderately intercorrelated (Spearman rho = .62, p < .001).

Table 2 presents correlations between factors and study measures. McFadden's pseudo-R² was 0.04, indicating that the model accounted for a small amount of variance (Cohen, 2013).

Results from Model 2 indicated that the Connection and Positive Emotions factor score was associated with greater positive persisting effects (B = 6.46, β = .30, SE = 1.50, t = 4.30, 95% CI [3.79, 9.13], p < .001), whereas the Time, Space and Self-Transcendence factor score was not (B = 1.05, β = .05, SE = 1.44, t = 0.73, 95% CI [-1.62, 3.73], p = .46). Adjusted R² was .11, indicating low variance accounted for by the model.

Regarding Models 3-6-which examined the relationship between factor scores and mindset at the time of the substance use experience-both factors were associated with greater state of surrender (Connection/Positive Emotion factor: B = 0.28, β = .34, SE = 0.04, t = 6.77, 95% CI [.20, .37], p < .001; Space/Time/Self-Transcendence factor: B = 0.31, β = .38, SE = 0.04, t = 7.09, 95% CI [.23, .40], p < .001), with this model accounting for a moderate amount of variance (Adjusted R² = .43). Similarly, both factors were associated with greater spiritual-prosocial motivations (Connection/Positive Emotion factor: B = 0.62, β = .38, SE = 0.09, t = 7.02, 95% CI [.46, .80], p < .001; Space/Time/Self-Transcendence factor: B = 0.49, β = .29, SE = 0.09, t = 5.53, 95% CI [.32, .66], p < .001), with this model accounting for a moderate amount of variance (Adjusted R² = .37).

Factors showed distinct associations with outcomes for models involving apprehensiveness, clarity of intention, and primary purpose for use. While Connection/Positive Emotion was associated with lower apprehensiveness at time of ingestion (B = -0.49, Odds Ratio (OR) = 0.61, SE = 0.13, t = -3.66, 95% CI [-0.76. -0.23], p < .001), the Space/Time/Self-Transcendence factor was associated with greater apprehensiveness (B = .93, OR = 2.54, SE = 0.14, t = 6.83, 95% CI [0.67.1.20], p < .001).

The Connection/Positive Emotion showed a small, statistically significant association with greater clarity of intentions at time of ingestion (B = .17, β = .19, SE = 0.06, t = 2.87, 95% CI [.06, .27], p = .004), whereas this association was small and nonsignificant for the Space/Time/Self-Transcendence factor (B = .10, β = .11, SE = 0.05, t = 1.63, 95% CI [-.01, .21], p = .10). Finally, while the Connection/Positive Emotion factor was associated with greater likelihood of having had a therapeutic or healing purpose for use (B = 0.70, OR = 2.01, SE = 0.22, z = 3.16, 95% CI [0.30, 1.12], p = .002), the Space/Time/Self-Transcendence factor was associated with lower likelihood of such purposes for use (B = -0.59, OR = 0.56, SE = 0.19, z = -3.16, 95% CI [-0.97, -0.21], p < .002).

Discussion

The present study sought to clarify the higher-order organization of psychedelicoccasioned self-transcendent experiences, and to examine whether these distinctions show meaningful associations with mindset, acute affective responses, and persisting positive effects. Drawing on measures of self-transcendent experience, self-transcendent emotion, mystical-type experience, small self, and self-other overlap, an exploratory factor analysis yielded two correlated but distinct components. One factor, labelled Connection and Positive Emotions, was characterized by connection-oriented self-transcendent experiences, selftranscendent and positive emotions, and greater inclusion of others in the self. The second factor, labelled Time, Space, and Self-Transcendence, reflected elements of self-transcendent experience characterized by loss of sense of self, distortions of time and space, and ineffability. These components showed distinct patterns of associations with outcomes-with only the Connection and Positive Emotions factor corresponding to beneficial outcomesunderscoring the importance of fine-grained assessment to differentiate between qualitatively distinct forms of self-transcendent experiences.

Self-Transcendent Experiences Under Psychedelics as Multifaceted

Both factors of self-transcendent experiences were moderately-to-strongly intercorrelated (ρ = .65), consistent with the blended phenomenology of subjective psychedelic experiences having a "common core" (MacLean et al., 2012; Stace, 1960; Watts et al., 2022). For instance, psychedelic experiences often appear to involve both a loosening of self-boundaries and an enhanced sense of affective connection and unity. Yet, the factors showed differential relations with affective responses during the experience and with persisting positive outcomes. This pattern aligns with theoretical perspectives proposing that self-transcendent/mystical experiences are multifaceted, comprising interrelated yet separable components (Cova & Seragnoli, 2025; Wittmann, 2015; Yaden et al., 2017b), as well as with prior empirical work demonstrating that self-transcendent experiences characterized by selfloss versus connection show distinct associations (Cova & Abatista, 2025; Yaden, 2020a).

Broad total scores assessing wide-ranging constructs (e.g., mystical-type experiences, oceanic boundlessness) provide a useful, big-picture overview of psychedelic effects; however, they can obscure fine-grained distinctions among experiential facets and may limit the field's ability to link specific phenomenological components to distinct mechanisms of action and therapeutic levers if not used in tandem with other granular assessment (Yaden et al., 2024). We recommend that assessments of altered states include not only total scores but also subscale-level information, supplemented by targeted measures of theorized mechanisms of change (e.g., connectedness, Davis et al., 2021; psychological insight, Watts et al., 2022; awe, Yaden et al., 2018; self-transcendent emotion, Fredrickson et al., 2003a). Supporting this recommendation, research has found that the explanatory power of the MEQ30 is increased when other dimensions-connectedness, paradoxicality-are added (Stocker et al., 2024). Overall, findings suggest that integrating granular assessments of specific facets of altered and self-transcendent experiences with traditional mystical measures may better isolate the phenomenological elements most relevant to enduring clinical change.

Connection and Positive Emotion Factor

The Connection and Positive Emotions factor identified in this study overlaps with several other constructs delineated in past empirical and conceptual work, including the relational or connection component of self-transcendent experiences (Yaden, 2020b; Yaden et al., 2017b), the vastness component of small self and awe, in which one feels a part of something grand, powerful, or greater than oneself (Tyson et al., 2022; Yaden et al., 2018), connectedness to self, others and the world (Watts et al., 2022), and "extroverted mysticism" or a sense of unity with the external world (Stace, 1960).

At the same time, the Connection and Positive Emotions factor integrates this relational-unitive quality with an explicitly affective dimension: overall positive emotions (e.g., bliss, peace) and self-transcendent emotions (awe, gratitude, inspiration, love, and sympathy). Positive emotions and self-transcendent emotions are often measured separately from experiences of interconnectedness (Fredrickson et al., 2003a; Gordon et al., 2017).

However, self-transcendent emotions are closely theoretically linked to relational experiences, such as through reducing self-focus, fostering a sense of common humanity, and promoting prosocial concern for others and the world (Gordon et al., 2017). For instance, awe may entail a sense of self-expansion, self-diminishment or connectedness (Yaden et al., 2018), gratitude supports relational health (Algoe et al., 2013) and love/compassion increase warmth, affiliation and bonding (Förster & Kanske, 2022). While positive emotions that are not explicitly self-transcendent are less directly tied to experiences of unity, they may nevertheless support feelings of connection by broadening attention and fostering interpersonal openness (Fredrickson, 2013).

That connection and positive and self-transcendent emotions loaded together in the current study suggests that such emotions may be part of the experiential "blueprint" of altered states characterized by a sense of interconnectedness, and that treating them as entirely distinct may underrepresent how these experiences are lived. Our work aligns with recent work postulating that self-transcendent emotions are central to psychedelic-induced experiences (Cova & Seragnoli, 2025), as well as finding that everyday experiences of unity are characterized by the presence of social emotions, such as compassion and love (Cova & Abatista, 2025), whereas these emotions were less characteristic of self-loss experiences.

It's important to note that contemplative and philosophical accounts highlight that experiences of interconnection can be accompanied not only by bliss and compassion, but also by contact with suffering. For instance, Thich Nhat Hanh's description of "interbeing" captures how a deep sense of shared existence can expose one to others' pain as well as their joy (e.g., "If you suffer, I suffer. If you are not safe, I am not safe") (Hanh, 2017). The present study did not include such dimensions in the factor analysis; future work could examine how connection, positive emotion, and painful affect co-occur within selftranscendent experiences.

Time, Space, and Self-Transcendence Factor

The Time, Space, and Self-Transcendence factor identified in the present study overlaps with constructs delineated in past empirical and conceptual work, such as descriptions of dissolving temporal and spatial boundaries and ineffability during psychedelic states (MacLean et al., 2012), the annihilational or self-loss component of self-transcendent experiences (Yaden, 2020b; Yaden et al., 2017b), and ego dissolution (though this construct also blends feelings of oneness/connection) (Nour et al., 2016). This factor aligns closely with the concept of "introverted mysticism," described as an ineffable experience of undifferentiated unity that involves the complete dissolution of the ego, subject-object distinctions and sensory content (Stace, 1960). Our work also aligns with research in time perception; for instance, Wittman describes how bodily states (affective, interoceptive) are inherently intertwined with time perception, such that diminished bodily awareness and selfreferential processing can contribute to feelings of timelessness (Wittmann, 2015).

Consistent with these conceptualizations, our findings suggest that dissolutions of time, space, and self tend to co-occur, representing a unified perceptual-cognitive process in which the usual anchor points from which human experience is referenced fade together. This co-occurrence aligns with recent findings from Cova & Abatista (2025) in which everyday experiences characterized by a sense of self-loss were associated with disruptions in the perception of space and time to a greater degree than experiences characterized by a sense of unity/connection. Of note, the co-occurrence of time, space and self-dissolution contrasts with Yaden and colleagues' (2017) premise that relational self-transcendent experiences, versus self-loss self-transcendent experiences, may encompass spatial unity, based upon theories linking social and spatial unity (Parkinson et al., 2014).

Links to mindset, acute affect, and persisting effects

Both components of self-transcendent experiences were robustly associated with aspects of intention and mindset at the time of substance ingestion. Connection and Positive Emotions showed consistent associations with greater spiritual-prosocial motivations, higher clarity of intentions, greater state of surrender, greater likelihood of having had a primarily therapeutic/healing purpose for use, as well as lower apprehensiveness at time of ingestion.

While Time, Space, and Self-Transcendence was similarly positively linked with spiritualprosocial motivations and surrender, it was associated with greater apprehensiveness at time of ingestion, with a lower likelihood of having used the substance for therapeutic/healing purposes and had a small nonsignificant association with clarity of intentions. These patterns suggest that spiritual or prosocial orientations and a stance of surrender may set the stage for both forms of self-transcendent experiences, whereas therapeutic/healing intentions for use, lower initial apprehensiveness, and to a lesser extent, clarity of intentions, may be especially conducive to affectively positive and connection-laden experiences. From a therapeutic standpoint, careful preparation around apprehension and fear-normalizing challenging experiences and helping clients relate differently to them-may be particularly important when aiming to facilitate self-transcendent experiences involving a sense of positive emotion and connection.

The two factors also showed distinct relationships with affect during the experience and persisting positive effects afterwards. Connection and Positive Emotions was associated with fewer negative emotions acutely and with greater self-reported positive persisting effects. In contrast, Time, Space, and Self-Transcendence predicted more intense negative emotions during the experience and was not associated with positive persisting effects. This overall pattern aligns with empirical work finding that experiences characterized by a mystical quality, sense of connection, expansion or positive mood are associated with beneficial outcomes, whereas experiences predominantly characterized by a loss of sense of self, time and space, ineffability, and small self-size are not (Barrett et al., 2015; Cova & Abatista, 2025; McCulloch et al., 2022; Tyson et al., 2022; Yaden, 2020a). These findings are also consistent with a recent systematic review of ego-dissolution and connectedness measures in classical psychedelic studies, which found that connectedness was associated with more durable mental health and well-being outcomes, whereas the effects of egodissolution were typically shorter-term (Kałużna et al., 2022).

Overall, our findings suggest that connection-and emotion-laden experiences appear more consistently aligned with positive persisting effects and lower acute negative affect.

Although causal inferences cannot be drawn from the present cross-sectional design, these associations are consistent with the possibility that fostering conditions that support connection, positive self-transcendent emotions, and a sense of interconnectedness may be particularly important for maximizing the lasting benefits of psychedelic experiences and for buffering against distress. This interpretation aligns with theories of positive affect, such as broaden-and-build, which posit that positive emotions expand attentional and cognitive scope and facilitate the accumulation of enduring psychological and social resources (Huppert et al., 2004). Psychedelic experiences may similarly engender broadened perspectives on self, others, and meaning, with downstream consequences for wellbeing. Complementing this account, research on social connection and belonging highlights that feeling embedded in supportive relationships and larger social contexts promotes perceived safety and reduces threat sensitivity (Gilbert, 2024). Consistent with this framework, the observed associations between the Connection and Positive Emotions factor, spiritual-prosocial motivations, lower apprehensiveness, and fewer negative emotions suggest that this experiential profile may reflect a state of heightened social and existential safeness, in which feelings of connection and positive affect buffer acute distress and support enduring psychological benefits.

Limitations and Future Directions

This study should be interpreted in light of its limitations. First, it relied on retrospective self-reports of an experience up to five years prior. Memory biases and post-hoc meaning-making may have influenced reports of the experience and its persisting effects.

Prospective, longitudinal designs that assess self-transcendent experiences and outcomes closer to real time would provide a stronger basis for causal inference. Second, most participants endorsed recreational rather than therapeutic motives and given the small impact of substance type on outcomes observed in the current study (redacted-for-anonymizedreview), experiences involving cannabis, MDMA, and psilocybin were combined. Although this diversity supports the generality of the identified components across substances and contexts, it limits direct generalization to clinical psychedelic-assisted therapies. Future work should examine whether similar factor structures and associations emerge in formal treatment contexts. Furthermore, although the factor solution showed good fit and internal adequacy, it was derived from a single sample; replication and confirmatory factor analyses are needed to establish its robustness and generalizability. Finally, the modest variance explained in negative emotions and positive persisting effects models reminds us that self-transcendent experiences are only one set of influences among many-including other subjective experiences (e.g., emotional breakthrough, psychological insight; Kangaslampi, 2023), integration processes, social context, broader life circumstances-that shape long-term outcomes.

Several measure-related considerations bear noting. Some constructs (e.g., small self, self-other overlap) were represented by single or few items; more comprehensive measurement of these domains may reveal additional nuance in their relations to other selftranscendent components. Moreover, the present study included a relatively small subset of measures. While this approach reduced item redundancy and response fatigue, future work could include other related measures, such as the ego dissolution inventory (Nour et al., 2016), Watt's connectedness scale (Watts et al., 2022) or the Awe Experience Scale (Yaden et al., 2018) to evaluate the robustness and generalizability of the observed factor structure.

Relatedly, future studies would benefit from assessing a broader range of conceptually related constructs (e.g., spiritual experiences, somatic experiences, perceived meaningfulness) to determine whether additional dimensions may form part of the phenomenological blueprint of self-transcendent experience. Somatic experiences (e.g., chills, goosebumps, shaking, physical connectedness), in particular, have been identified as a core phenomenological feature of self-transcendent emotions and psychedelic experiences in prior qualitative and theoretical work (Garcia-Romeu et al., 2015; Yaden et al., 2018), yet were not assessed in this study. Finally, incorporating a wider array of measures-including measures not commonly administered within psychedelic research (as we did with the Small Self, Inclusion of Self in Other and modified Differential Emotion scales)-may further bridge psychedelic science with broader contemplative, affective, and transcendental literatures.

Future research could build on the present findings by testing whether connection/positive emotion-related versus dissolution-related experiences differentially mediate symptom or wellbeing outcomes, by experimentally manipulating aspects of set and setting hypothesized to preferentially foster specific types of subjective experiences, and by examining how challenging self-transcendent experiences interact with integration and support processes to yield growth versus harm. Although our data are purely phenomenological and do not test underlying mechanisms, they point to the value of future work examining whether distinct neurological mechanisms may underlie experiences characterized by Connection and Positive Emotions versus Time, Space, and Self-Transcendence. How psychedelic-induced subjective experiences are linked to neurobiological or perceptual factors, such as "brain entropy" (Rankaduwa & Owen, 2023), deictic or perspective-taking processes (Hayes et al., 2001), or changes in functional connectivity within association networks, such as the default-mode network (Kwan et al., 2022), remains an open area of inquiry (Yu et al., 2024).

Conclusion

In summary, this study provides initial evidence that psychedelic-occasioned selftranscendent experiences can be meaningfully organized into at least two correlated higherorder components-one centered on connection and positive emotions, and another on loss of one's sense of time, space boundaries, and self. These components show distinct relationships with mindset, acute affect, and persisting positive effects, supporting a multidimensional conceptualization of self-transcendent and mystical experiences.
